interpretation: Keeping the frozen fit100 classifiers and calibration but feeding EVAL rows history/profile features computed from all strictly-prior 2026 games (H2) lowers EVAL NLL by 0.00177 (CI95 [-0.00236, -0.00119]) and Brier by 0.00056 (CI below 0); even the operationally simpler pre-series freeze (H1, history frozen at CAL end) gives -0.00127. For scale, this exceeds the recorded fit100-vs-OLD NLL gain (-0.00128) without any refit. The gain concentrates where history was missing: pitchers with no FIT-period 2026 history (S0, 66 pitchers / 7,699 pitches) improve by -0.0060 NLL (CI [-0.0088, -0.0031]) and their own-outcome-missing fraction drops from 100% to 22%; batters unseen in FIT improve by -0.0075. Pitchers with >= 1000 FIT rows show no significant change (-0.0007, CI covers 0). Top-label ECE differences have CIs covering zero overall but the S0 ECE point value halves (0.0163 -> 0.0110). Causal reading: the FIT-frozen features created a train/serve staleness mismatch (FIT rows were trained with fresh strictly-prior history), and removing it helps. LIMITS: 2026 EXPOSED DEVELOPMENT, no independent TEST; no refit (a prequential-refit arm is a follow-up); the history pool is 2026-only, so S0 means no 2026 FIT-period history, not no <=2025 record; this is the research fit100 model, not the serving G0/ARM-B path, so the 11 unsupported roster pitchers are not covered by this result — but it is direct evidence that a nightly strictly-prior profile update is the cheapest lever for low-history pitchers. Fan-facing meaning: for pitchers the model has barely seen, next-pitch outcome probabilities get measurably sharper when yesterday's games are counted; for established pitchers the change is within noise.
